analysis.one_liner: Keeps employer health coverage intact for workers during strikes and lockouts.
analysis.headline: The bill sits in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee with 14 cosponsors — all Democrats or independents — and no hearing, markup, or vote since it was referred on June 5, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it an unfair labor practice for an employer to terminate or change a worker's employer-provided health coverage during a lawful strike or a lockout. It would add federal fines of up to $75,000 per violation for lockouts and $50,000 per strike, doubling to $150,000 and $100,000 for repeat offenders who cause serious harm, and would let regulators fine individual directors and officers. It was introduced in June 2025 and has not moved since it was referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers on strike or locked out, and their families, who would keep their employer health coverage instead of losing it mid-dispute — often the moment when a serious illness or a prescription becomes a financial crisis. Unions also gain, because an employer could no longer use cut-off coverage as pressure in bargaining.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Striking and locked-out workers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Amends the National Labor Relations Act so that terminating or altering an employee's group health plan coverage during a lockout or a lawful strike is an unfair labor practice, which the National Labor Relations Board can prosecute.

Creates civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation for coverage terminations during a lockout and up to $50,000 per violation during a lawful strike, doubled to $150,000 and $100,000 when a repeat offender's action coincides with a discharge or causes serious economic harm.

Allows the Board to assess penalties directly against a company's directors or officers who directed, committed, or had the authority to prevent a violation and failed to do so — putting the consequence on decision-makers rather than only the company.
Requires the Board to weigh the gravity of the employer's conduct, its effect on workers exercising their rights, the employer's size, and its history of violations when setting penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially those with unionized workforces — who would have to keep funding group health coverage through strikes and lockouts, would face fines per violation, and could see personal penalties on executives. The cost is real but limited to disputes: coverage continues only for the duration of the strike or lockout.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes one form of employer leverage in a labor dispute: cutting off health coverage to pressure workers. Employers and management-side groups would argue this shifts bargaining power toward unions and makes strikes and lockouts more expensive to sustain, potentially lengthening disputes.

Penalties up to $150,000 per violation, plus possible personal liability for directors and officers, create new litigation and compliance exposure that would weigh most heavily on smaller employers with thinner margins.

The protection only covers employer-sponsored group health plans, so workers whose coverage is not tied to their job — or who have already lost it — get nothing from this bill; it leaves the underlying dependence of health care on employment untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers affected, the benefit is concrete and severe: losing health coverage mid-strike can mean unpickable prescriptions or uncovered hospital bills at exactly the moment a family has no paycheck. The cost falls on employers in the narrow window of a dispute and is capped by the penalty structure, though it does change bargaining leverage and adds compliance burden. The bill is narrow and targeted rather than sweeping; its main weakness is that it patches one gap in employment-based coverage without addressing the structure that creates the gap.

outcome.mechanism: It has sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on June 5, 2025, joined by ten original cosponsors including Sanders, Warren, Fetterman, and Blumenthal.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
It has since drawn 14 cosponsors — 13 Senate Democrats and 1 independent — and the action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use health coverage cut-offs as leverage in labor disputes are better off, because the option remains open and no penalties attach. Workers on strike or locked out gained nothing.

against.name: 55 of 55 Senate Republicans

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors are Senate Democrats or independents and no Republican has signed on; no vote has occurred, so the only recorded opposition is the majority's inaction.

industries.industry: Employers with unionized workforces (manufacturing, logistics, food processing)
industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to cut health coverage during a strike or lockout and attaches fines of up to $150,000 per violation, including possible personal penalties on executives. For workers, this is the difference between keeping coverage and losing it at their most financially vulnerable moment.

Unions gain bargaining strength because an employer could no longer pressure members by terminating health coverage mid-dispute. This interest runs alongside members' own interest in keeping coverage.

industries.industry: Health insurers and benefits plan administrators
industries.note: Coverage continuing through a strike or lockout means premiums keep flowing during disputes. The bill does not regulate insurers, so their position is essentially unchanged except for the preserved revenue.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, chairing the HELP Committee, and no Republican cosponsor, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or a floor vote this Congress. Absent a change in the Senate's composition or a high-profile strike that forces the issue, it will most likely die in committee when the Congress ends, as similar labor bills have.
